activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Slow breathing with long exhales can calm the body's stress response, which is why it is a common coping skill before a stressful moment.
story:
The clock on Mr. Smith's desk said 2:58, and Jeremy stared at it like it might run backward if he wished hard enough. In two minutes he would be sitting across from Mr. Smith, the guidance counsellor, explaining why he had thrown a pencil sharpener at the gym door. He hadn't hit anyone. That was the one good thing. The bad thing was that everyone had seen him do it, including Adriana, whose opinion of him mattered more than he wanted to admit.

"Jeremy," Mr. Smith said, gesturing to the squishy blue chair, "before we get to the sharpener, tell me about tryouts." Mr. Smith was an influential figure at their school, the one teacher even the eighth graders listened to, and somehow he already knew everything. "Soccer, right? Saturday?"

Jeremy sat. "Goalie tryouts." His hands were sweating again, the way they had all week. "I keep messing up in practice. My stomach hurts, my hands shake, and I can't think. Maximiliano says I'm just nervous, but it feels bigger than that."

"That sounds like stress," Mr. Smith said. "Sometimes anxiety shows up in the body before you notice it in your head." He wrote the word anxiety on a sticky note and slid it across the desk. "And this?" He tapped a poster on the wall that said COPING SKILLS in block letters. "These are things people learn to do before a hard moment. Not medicine, nothing a doctor prescribes. Just skills."

Jeremy studied the poster. Box breathing. Counting. Slow breathing with long exhales. He thought about Saturday, about facing a penalty shot, and a memory surfaced that he hadn't connected to anything until now. His uncle, who had served overseas and now coached a youth league in a civilian neighborhood two towns over, always stood behind the net before shootouts. Jeremy had watched him once, breathing out slowly, so slowly, through puckered lips, while the shooter lined up.

"Wait," Jeremy said slowly, testing the idea like ice on a pond. "My uncle breathes like that before every penalty shot. Long exhales. I thought it was superstition, like not stepping on the foul line." He stood up. "It's not superstition. It's a skill. It calms the body down before the stressful moment." He tried it right there, in the office, a slow breath in and a long breath out, and his stomach unclenched just a little, enough to notice.

Mr. Smith smiled and mentioned boundaries, about knowing what was his to control and what belonged to the coach's decisions, but Jeremy was barely listening. He asked to borrow the poster. On Saturday, standing in the goal, Jeremy took one slow breath and let it out so long that the shooter paused and looked at him, confused. The ball sailed straight into Jeremy's gloves, and from the sideline he heard Adriana shout, "Nice save, superstition boy!"

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Parallel lines like railway tracks or the two edges of a road look as if they meet in the distance, even though they never actually meet.
story:
Romy sat at the kitchen table with a pencil, a ruler, and a blank page that was starting to feel like an enemy. Her art teacher, Mr. Bouchard, had promised the class that anyone who mastered one-point perspective could design the backdrop for the spring play, and Romy wanted that job more than she had wanted anything since the talent show in grade five. The trouble was the vanishing point. Every time she drew her street, the buildings looked like they were falling over sideways.

She called Fatimah, who showed up ten minutes later with her own sketchbook and a bag of pretzels, because Fatimah never went anywhere without snacks. "Okay," Fatimah said, dropping into the chair across the table, "show me the disaster."

Romy turned her page around. Fatimah leaned in to scrutinize the drawing, tilting her head first one way and then the other. "The road edges are wrong," she said at last. "They don't go to the same place."

"They do too," Romy said, but she grabbed her ruler and laid it along one edge, then the other. The two lines crossed somewhere off the corner of the page. Fatimah was right. "They're supposed to meet at the vanishing point," Romy muttered, "but I put the point in two different spots without noticing."

Fatimah pulled out her phone and swiped through her photos until she found one from last summer, a shot of train tracks taken from the footbridge near her grandmother's house. She slid the phone across the table. "Look at this. The rails look like they touch way out there."

Romy peered at the picture. "They look closer in the distance, sure."

"No, they look like they meet," Fatimah insisted. "Like they actually come together."

"They can't meet," Romy said. "They're parallel. Rails are the same distance apart the whole way, or the train would fall off." Fatimah frowned at the photo, clearly not convinced, so Romy took the ruler and measured the rails near the bottom of the picture, then the same rails farther back. Near, the gap was wide; far away, it shrank to almost nothing. "See? They only look like they meet. Parallel lines like railway tracks, or the two edges of a road, look as if they meet in the distance, even though they never actually meet."

Fatimah grabbed a pretzel and chewed on it along with the idea. "So that's why my drawing looked flat," she said. "I drew the road edges the same distance apart the whole way." She had been hoping for the backdrop job too, and suddenly her shoulders drooped.

Romy looked at her friend's sketchbook, then at her own ruined street. "Draw with me," she said. "We'll both get good at it, and whoever wins, the other one helps paint." Fatimah's face brightened. They pushed the pretzels aside, taped a fresh sheet to the table, and marked a single dot in the middle of the page.

"Every edge of the road goes to that dot," Romy said, and drew her first line straight toward it.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: The Koppen climate classification, still used on climate maps today, was developed by Wladimir Koppen, a climatologist born in Russia who worked in Germany.
story:
Katherine had the graphs spread across two airport seats while the departure board flickered from ON TIME to DELAYED. Rainfall bars for a rainforest station rose like green towers every month, while the desert station barely showed a sliver all year, and the temperature lines told their own story, one steady and warm, the other swinging between baking days and cold nights. Her worksheet asked her to compare the two climates, but the second page had a climate map of the world with strange letter codes printed over each region, Af here, BWh there, and she had no idea what they meant. If she did not finish before they boarded, Ms. Kovalenko would mark it late, and Katherine refused to be negligent about the one assignment she actually found interesting.

Ziyad dropped into the seat beside her with two pretzels and handed her one. "Stuck?"

"These codes," Katherine said, tapping the map. "Af, BWh. They must mean something, because the rainforest is always Af and the deserts are always B, but I can't test that if I don't know who made the rules or why."

Teagan leaned over from the other side, chewing. "Ask your phone."

"It's in my checked bag with my charger," Katherine said, which was exactly the kind of planning she could not justify to anyone. She looked around the gate area instead, and spotted the tiny airport bookshop with its rack of atlases. She ran over, found a world atlas, and flipped to the climate map section, following the tiny print to a note at the bottom.

"Listen to this," she said, hurrying back and reading aloud. "The codes are called the Koppen climate classification, still used on climate maps today. It was developed by Wladimir Koppen, a climatologist born in Russia who worked in Germany."

"So Af isn't random," Teagan said slowly.

"It's a system. Koppen looked at rainfall and temperature together, the exact things on my graphs." Katherine laid her hand flat over the map, covering the rainforest band. "See, everywhere with year-round rain and steady warmth gets Af. Every desert gets a B and something about how dry." She checked her graphs against the map three times, and the pattern held each time. She wrote her comparison, and then, feeling bolder, added the note about the codes and who invented them.

Ms. Kovalenko walked past, glanced at the paper, and smiled. "You did the bonus question. I hadn't even assigned it yet."

Katherine grinned and looked up just as the board changed again. The flight was cancelled, and their class trip to the rainforest would have to wait for tomorrow, leaving Katherine with a finished assignment comparing two climates, and no airplane to get to either of them. Teagan held out the last pretzel. "Deserts, at least, wait for everybody."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: A mirror ball turns one spotlight into hundreds of moving spots of light because each small mirror tile reflects the beam in a slightly different direction.
story:
Payton stood in the school parking lot with Jenny, both of them holding their dance tickets so tightly the paper had gone soft at the corners. The October wind smelled like someone's fallen leaves and bus exhaust, and through the gym doors they could already hear the thump of music.

"I'm not going in if it's going to be like last year's field day," Jenny said. "I hid in the restroom for an hour."

Payton remembered field day too. She flashed back to that afternoon in the parking lot, the exact spot where she was standing now, when the coach had asked her to run the relay anchor leg and she had frozen while the whole grade watched. She had spent the whole ride home trying to digest what had gone wrong, and she still wasn't sure. "This time we walk in together," she said. "We find a wall. Walls are safe."

Inside, the gym had been transformed. Somebody had hung a mirror ball from the ceiling, and the gym was full of small spots of light that swept across the floor, the bleachers, and the backs of everyone's heads. Payton and Jenny pressed themselves against the wall by the water fountain, exactly as planned.

Then Payton noticed something. When the ball turned, the spots all moved together, like a school of fish. She watched the single spotlight in the corner, the one Mr. Nikolaidis was adjusting on its stand, and then watched a spot of light slide up her own sneaker. When he switched the spotlight off, every spot vanished at once. When he switched it back on, hundreds of spots reappeared. So it wasn't hundreds of lights up there. Each little mirror tile on the ball caught that one beam and threw it in a slightly different direction, which was why the whole gym sparkled from a single bulb.

"Watch this," Payton said, and she waved at Mr. Nikolaidis, then pointed at the spotlight and made a turning motion with her finger. He grinned, gave a thumbs up, and spun the ball faster. The spots raced across the floor in long streaks.

"Okay, that's actually amazing," Jenny said. "How did you know he'd do that?"

"Because I watched what happened when he turned the light off and on. One spotlight, all those spots. It has to be the ball."

Imane wandered over from the snack table, where she claimed to have a monopoly on the pretzels since nobody else was eating them. "Are you two going to stand there all night studying physics, or are you going to dance?" She grabbed Jenny's wrist.

The opening notes of a song they all knew started up, and the spots of light came sweeping toward the wall like a wave. Payton pushed off the wall and stepped into the middle of them, sneakers and all, and called over her shoulder, "Come on, Jenny. Walls are for people who don't know how light works."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: Compound interest is paid on the principal plus all the interest already earned, so the interest itself starts earning interest.
story:
Every Saturday morning, Ava swept the floor of Mr. Xu's clock shop, dusted the shelves of tiny brass gears, and earned twelve dollars, which she carried straight to the bank on the corner. She had been doing this since September, and by spring she had saved two hundred and forty dollars. Her plan was simple: keep saving until she could buy the leather satchel in the window of the artisan shop down the street, the one the leatherworker had stitched by hand, with a brass clasp that matched the clock gears she spent her mornings dusting.

One Saturday the teller handed her a slip of paper with her balance, and Ava stared at it. Last month the bank had paid her interest, one dollar and twenty cents. This month it had paid one dollar and twenty-one cents. "That's bizarre," she said. "I didn't put anything extra in." She checked the deposit column twice, thinking she would find a mistake, a number she had forgotten. There was nothing. The same deposits, the same two hundred and forty dollars, and yet the interest itself had grown.

She took the problem to Harriet, who was waiting outside the shop with a bag of pistachios. "Look," Ava said, holding out the slip. "Same money in, more interest out." Harriet chewed a pistachio and squinted at the numbers. "Maybe the bank just felt generous," she said, which was exactly the kind of answer Harriet always gave. Ava shook her head. She remembered her grandmother once choosing an account that paid simple interest, the same flat amount every year, and regretting it, and Ava had never understood why until now. She flipped the slip over and found a small paragraph of fine print, and read it slowly, following the words with her finger.

Compound interest is paid on the principal plus all the interest already earned, she read, so the interest itself starts earning interest. She read it again. The one dollar and twenty cents from last month hadn't just sat there like a coin under a mattress. It had joined her two hundred and forty dollars, and together they had earned the extra penny. Her money was growing money. She thought about her grandmother's flat account, the same dollar every year for five years, never a penny more, and about the five years ahead of her own account, where each month's interest would climb onto the last month's and earn again.

"It's like the shop," she told Harriet, waving toward the window where the brass gears turned. "Each gear grabs the one beside it. The second one only moves because the first one moved." Harriet popped another pistachio. "So your money is a gear," she said. "Weird. But okay." Ava folded the slip and put it in her pocket, next to the satchel fund total she kept in her head. On the walk home she stopped in front of the artisan's window, looked at the brass clasp, and then kept walking, because she had just decided to leave her money where it could orbit on its own. "Five years," she said to Harriet. "Watch it turn."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Many places of worship, including mosques, Hindu temples and Sikh gurdwaras, ask visitors to remove their shoes, and gurdwaras also ask everyone to cover their head.
story:
Lincoln could hear the drums before he reached the park gates. It was Vaisakhi, and the whole community had spilled out of the gurdwara onto the grass, with stalls of food, kids chasing each other between blankets, and a stage where a group was singing. His mother had sent him with a bag of rice to donate, and she was somewhere behind him arguing cheerfully with an aunt about who made better pakoras.

At the edge of the crowd, Lincoln spotted Jessy from his science class, standing awkwardly near a shoe rack piled with hundreds of pairs of shoes. "You came," Lincoln said, surprised. Jessy shrugged. "You said there'd be food. Also I'm supposed to write about a cultural celebration for Ms. Mori's class, so this counts as research."

"We have to go inside the gurdwara to drop off the rice," Lincoln said, toeing off his sneakers and setting them on the rack. "You take your shoes off too. Everyone does, everywhere, in mosques and Hindu temples and gurdwaras. It's a respect thing." Jessy looked down at his battered shoes, whose laces had gone a strange greenish color from winter puddles, like something corrosive had been at them. He pulled them off anyway.

At the next door, Lincoln paused. He'd forgotten the one part that always tripped him up. A volunteer was handing out thin orange scarves, and every single person who passed through covered their head, whether they were a grandfather or a girl Jessy's age. Lincoln had gotten this wrong at Diwali two years ago, walking in bareheaded until his cousin yanked him back by the collar, and he wasn't going to let Jessy make the same mistake. "Here," he said, taking two scarves. "In a gurdwara you cover your head. Everyone, no exceptions." He tied his own the way his grandfather had taught him, a quick knot at the side.

Jessy fumbled with his, dropping one end in the dirt, and Lincoln stepped in and helped him loop it. "Like a concept in physics," Jessy said, adjusting it. "Once you know the rule, you can predict what happens at every door." They carried the rice inside, where the smell of dal and warm bread rolled over them, and a man with a kind face waved them toward the kitchen.

Later, on the grass, Jessy ate his third plate of food and scribbled notes for Ms. Mori, filling a whole page about shoes and scarves and the kitchens that feed anyone who shows up. "This is going to be the best report in the class," he said. Lincoln stole a piece of his bread and grinned. "You're welcome. Next time, dig deeper. There's a whole library in there." Jessy pointed his pen at him and said, "You mean excavate the truth?" and Lincoln laughed so hard the plate nearly slid off the blanket.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution says no person can be forced, in a criminal case, to be a witness against themselves.
story:
Alex had said "I plead the Fifth" eleven times that week, mostly to avoid taking out the trash, and it had worked exactly zero times, so he decided to find out what the phrase actually meant before the constitutional rights fair at city hall on Saturday.

Ms. Wiśniewski had assigned the fair weeks ago. Each student had to pick one right from the constitution, read it aloud, and explain it in their own words at a table in the rotunda, where real city employees would wander by and listen. Alex had drawn the Fifth Amendment out of the paper bag, and Abdulrahman had drawn the Second, and Dev had gotten the Tenth and kept mispronouncing it as "the Tent," which Alex privately found funnier than it was.

The night before the fair, Alex sprawled on his bedroom floor with the amendment copied out on index cards. He read it slowly, twice, and something clicked. "Wait," he said to the ceiling. "It says no person can be forced, in a criminal case, to be a witness against themselves. That's what it means. You can't be made to accuse yourself." Suddenly every courtroom show he had ever half-watched made sense. The silence on the shows wasn't rudeness; it was the rule itself. He tested the idea against a memory from last summer, when his cousin had confessed to breaking a neighbor's window just because an adult kept asking questions in a loud voice. If his cousin had known this, Alex thought, she could have just kept quiet. That was the whole consequence of not knowing your rights: you give them away by talking.

Saturday morning, the rotunda echoed with footsteps and the squeak of folding tables. Alex propped up his poster, which read PLEAD THE FIFTH in letters that Dev said looked "counterfeit, like a fake movie poster," and Alex took it as a compliment. Then the mayor's assistant stopped at his table, arms crossed, and said, "So, young man, if I asked you right now who left this coffee ring on the historical plaque, would you answer?"

Alex recognized the trap immediately, because the adult's smile implied there was only one right answer, and there were clearly two. He leaned forward. "In an actual criminal case, no. No person can be forced, in a criminal case, to be a witness against themselves. But this is city hall, not a courtroom, and the coffee ring is not a crime, so honestly? It was probably Dev."

"Hey!" Dev said from the next table, holding up his own coffee cup with mock horror.

Abdulrahman wandered over with a laminated copy of the constitution and a smuggled donut. "You realize you just snitched voluntarily," he said. "The Fifth only protects you if you stay quiet."

"That," Alex said, "is the best thing anyone has learned at this table all day." He straightened his poster, picked up a fresh index card, and began: "Okay, from the top. Somebody accuse me of something."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: According to the U.S. CDC, adults catch an average of two to three colds a year, and children often catch more.
story:
Nathaniel sat on the porch of his grandfather's house wrapped in a quilt that smelled like cedar and engine oil, blowing his nose for approximately the four hundredth time that morning. This was his third cold since fall, and he had begun to suspect something was wrong with him. He texted Soraya, who replied with a shrugging emoji and no help at all.

Inside, his grandfather was sanding a chair at the workbench in the kitchen, one of the contemporary designs he sold at the market on Saturdays. He called himself an artisan, which Nathaniel had once thought was just a fancy word for someone who refused to buy furniture like a normal person. The rhythemic scrape of sandpaper was the only sound until Nathaniel shuffled in and dropped onto a stool.

"Grandpa, can I borrow your laptop? Mine's dead and I need to look something up."

"Look up what?"

"Whether three colds since October means I'm dying."

His grandfather slid the laptop across the table without stopping his sanding. "Negotiate with me for it later. You're paying in firewood stacking."

Nathaniel typed his question and scrolled, tissues crumpled in his fist. The first result was from the CDC, which sounded official enough to trust. He read it twice, then a third time, because it said the opposite of what he expected. According to the CDC, adults catch an average of two to three colds a year, and children often catch more. He was fourteen, which put him somewhere between the two, and three colds since fall was not a mystery illness at all. It was practically average.

"Guess what," he said, wheeling the stool toward the workbench. "Adults get two to three colds a year on average, and kids get even more. I'm normal."

"Congratulations," his grandfather said dryly. "You've cured yourself with statistics."

Then came the twist Nathaniel hadn't planned. He scrolled a little further, still gloating, and found the CDC's page on handwashing. He thought about school, about the shared markers in art class, about how many times a day he touched his face. He had spent three months blaming his weak immune system, but the pattern might not be inside him at all. It might be on his hands. That night, when Soraya texted to ask if he was still alive, he wrote back, "Alive and washing my hands like it's my job. Also you owe me a pop, I bet you didn't know kids catch more colds than adults." He set the phone down, carried the quilt back to the porch, and watched the fireflies come out over the field.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The equality rights in section 15 of the Canadian Charter came into force in 1985, three years after the rest, to give governments time to update their laws.
story:
Colton had the photocopy of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms spread across his knees in the back row of the town hall, where the folding chairs smelled faintly of dust and lemon polish. His assignment, due Monday, was to explain one right in his own words at a class presentation, and Mr. Goldberg had suggested he come hear how real citizens actually talked about the Charter. Up front, a woman was asking the council something about a recreation fee, and Colton only half listened while he ran his pencil down the sections.

Then he noticed something odd. At the top of one page, in small print, section 15 was listed as coming into force in 1985, while the sections beside it had taken effect three years earlier, in 1982. He read it twice, then flipped back and forth to be sure he was not mixing up the dates. Why would one right arrive late, like a bus that missed its own schedule?

He leaned toward Jessa, who sat beside him with her own copy, chewing the cap of her pen. "Look at this," he whispered, pointing. "Equality rights, section 15. It says it didn't start until 1985. Everything else started in 1982."

Jessa squinted at the page. "That's ironic. The equality one, late." She tapped the paper. "Maybe it's a typo."

Colton tested the typo idea on the spot. If it were a typo, the same date should appear somewhere else, in a summary or a textbook, or it should not appear at all. When the meeting paused for the recreation fee vote, he raised his hand, mostly to see what would happen, and asked the mayor whether the Charter had taken effect in 1982 or 1985.

"1982," the mayor said, and half the room nodded, and a man near the front added, "Except section 15. That one waited three years, until 1985, so governments had time to bring their laws in line." Colton wrote it down quickly, the pencil hinge of his notebook creaking as he turned the page.

So it was real, and it was not a mistake. The rest of the Charter had started right away, and the equality rights had come into force in 1985, a three-year delay. The whole difference seemed to hinge on that gap, and Colton felt the shape of an explanation forming, though he could not yet justify it in words he would want to say out loud.

After the meeting, Josie caught up with them on the town hall steps, where the evening light lay long and orange across the concrete. "Find your right yet?" she asked.

"Better," Colton said, folding his photocopy with the section 15 page on the outside. "I found a puzzle."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Keith Johnstone's 1979 book 'Impro' taught that characters in a scene play higher or lower status, and shifting status creates drama.
story:
Emilie's scene kept dying. Every time she and Johan stepped into the circle at drama camp, he would offer something like "The spaceship is leaking air," and she would say, "No, actually, we're in a kitchen," because his ideas seemed dumb, and then the scene would just stop. Ms. MacLeod wrote on the whiteboard in big letters: yes, and. "Accept every offer and add to it," she said, and then she picked partners out of the coffee can, and Emilie got Johan again, which meant she had one afternoon to figure out how to stop killing scenes before the final showcase for the parents.

At lunch she sat alone under the oak tree to isolate the problem. It wasn't that his ideas were bad. It was that she always played the person in charge, the captain, the famous scientist, and whoever was in charge got to say no. She'd seen it happen in every failed scene this week. She flipped through the battered book Ms. MacLeod left on the bench, a 1979 thing called "Impro" by a man named Keith Johnstone, and one idea jumped out at her: characters in a scene play higher or lower status, and shifting status creates drama. She read it twice. That was the pattern. That was the hidden rule nobody had named out loud.

For the afternoon rehearsal, she proposed a king-and-servant scene. "I'll be the king," Johan said immediately, thrilled to finally have a prestigious role. "Fine," Emilie said, and something in her chest twisted, but she bowed low and began polishing an imaginary crown. The scene was flat for about a minute. Then Emilie, still holding the polishing cloth, said, "Hold still. Your collar is crooked, and you will not see the ambassador until it's fixed." Johan blinked, then straightened like a scolded kid. "But the ambassador is waiting," he said meekly. "The ambassador," Emilie announced, "will wait, and afterward you will apologize to the cook for sending back the soup." The kids watching cracked up. The servant was giving orders, the king was obeying, and the scene was alive. When the king tried to reclaim the throne, ordering a tariff on all jellybeans in the kingdom, the servant countered by confiscating his scepter until he ate his vegetables, and Madyson laughed so hard she fell off her chair.

The showcase went even better, until the last moment, when the audience was still clapping and Johan stepped to the front and took the bow by himself. Emilie stood half in the shadows behind him, holding the polishing cloth. Maybe he didn't think. Maybe he did.

Ms. MacLeod caught her at the door. "Next session, I want you two writing your own two-person show," she said. "You've got something." Emilie glanced across the parking lot to where Johan was climbing into his mom's car, not looking back. "Yeah," she said. "We do." She pulled the old copy of "Impro" out of her bag, the page on status still marked, and wondered whether she'd lend it to him on Monday or keep it to herself.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: A control group in an experiment gets everything the test group gets except the thing being tested, so any difference between the groups can be linked to that one thing.
story:
At dinner Romy pushed her noodles around and told her mother about the argument. Rosa had brought a small paper packet to science class and announced that her grandmother's special fertilizer made plants grow twice as fast. She had one photo of a tall green bean plant on her grandmother's windowsill, and she had passed the packet around so everyone could smell it. "She says it works because her plant got huge," Romy said. "But Zacharie said his uncle grew a giant pumpkin with no fertilizer at all. So who's right?" Her mother asked whether anyone had tested it. Nobody had. Ms. Foster had given them until Friday to settle it, and Romy wanted to be the one to settle it.

After dinner she inhaled the last of her garlic bread, thanked her mother, and carried four identical pots to the table where the window let in good light. She filled each pot with the same soil from the same bag, pressed in two bean seeds per pot, and measured out the same water into a small jug so every pot got exactly the same amount. Then she wrote on masking tape: Pot One, fertilizer. Pot Two, fertilizer. Pot Three, no fertilizer. Pot Four, no fertilizer.

Her mother leaned in the doorway with a dish towel. "Why the extras? One pot with and one without would tell you something."

"Two of each is better," Romy said. She set the packets aside. "The ones with fertilizer get everything the others get, sunlight, water, soil, the same spot on the table. Only the fertilizer is different. Then if the fertilized pots grow taller, it can't be because of the water or the light. It has to be the fertilizer." She tapped the tape on Pot Three. "These two are my control group."

"Control group," her mother repeated. "Like in the article about the new cold medicine?"

"Exactly like that," Romy said. She slid all four pots to the same end of the table where the light was even.

At school on Friday, Rosa's packet sat unopened on the lab bench next to Romy's pots, and the bean seedlings stood in a neat row. Rosa had counted on her fingers for a while, then had gone quiet when she measured the control pots. Zacharie leaned over with the ruler, and Ms. Foster wrote the four numbers on the board.

"So it does work," Rosa said slowly, looking at the two taller rows of seedlings.

"It works," Romy said, "but your grandmother's one plant couldn't tell us that. One plant is just one plant. It could have been the window, or the seed, or just luck." She turned Pot Three so its shorter leaves faced Rosa. "This pot got everything your plant got except the fertilizer. That's how we know."

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: In German, a customer can ask for the bill by saying "Die Rechnung, bitte," meaning "The bill, please."
story:
Gavin sat at the corner table in the school library with a menu written in German, the same kind Ms. Hu had handed out for the class trip lunch on Friday. He could already order food. He had practiced "Ich möchte das Hähnchen" until Ashton told him to stop saying chicken in his sleep. What he could not do was figure out how to ask for the bill, because the phrase list Ms. Hu had given them cut off right after the food vocabulary, and the class would only have fifty minutes for lunch before the museum tour.

"You're still on that?" Ashton asked, dropping into the chair across from him. "Just point at your wallet when the waiter comes."

"That obstructs the whole table," Gavin said. "If we sit there pointing, we're late, and Ms. Hu makes everyone else wait." He flipped through the German dictionary, but he did not even know what word to look up. Bill? Check? Paper?

Armin slid his laptop over. "Look, I found a video where a family eats at a restaurant in Berlin. Maybe somebody pays in it."

They watched three minutes of people ordering schnitzel, and then, just as Gavin was about to give up, the father raised his hand and said something that sounded fast but clear. Gavin backed the video up and played it twice more. "Die Rechnung, bitte," he said slowly. He checked the dictionary. "Rechnung. It means the bill."

"So that's it?" Ashton said. "That's how you ask?"

"That's how you ask," Gavin said. "The bill, please."

The trouble was knowing it and saying it under pressure were two different things, so Gavin invented a test. Every time someone approached their table in the library, he had to say the phrase before he lost his nerve. The first time, when Armin came back from the shelves, Gavin blurted "Die Rechnung, bitte" so loudly that a boy two tables over looked up. The second time was smoother. By the time Ms. Hu walked past on her way to the front desk, Gavin raised his hand and said it calmly, and she smiled without breaking stride.

On Friday, at the little restaurant near the museum, the meal ran long because the kitchen was slow and everyone argued about splitting the dessert. Gavin watched the clock on the wall creep toward the time they had to leave, and his stomach tightened. Then he caught the waiter's eye, lifted his hand, and said, "Die Rechnung, bitte."

The waiter nodded and returned with the bill in under a minute. Ashton leaned over and whispered, "Okay, that was the most fundamental thing anyone has done all trip."

"Better than a pointing treaty with the waiter?" Gavin asked.

"Way better," Ashton said, and slid his share across the table.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: 1 is not a prime number; mathematicians exclude it so that every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes.
story:
Nevaeh had been staring at her laptop for twenty minutes, and the blinking cursor in the Python file seemed almost predatory, waiting for her to make a mistake. Her program was supposed to ask for a number and print whether it was prime, and it worked fine for 7 and 13 and even 97. Then she had typed 1, and the screen had said PRIME, and something about that felt wrong. Last summer she had argued with her cousin at a picnic about almost the same thing, and she had lost the argument because she'd laughed at the wrong moment. She wasn't going to lose this one.

She texted Madeline, who was doing the same coding project at her own house three streets away.

"does your program say 1 is prime," Nevaeh typed.

"yeah. is that bad?" came the answer, followed by a shrug emoji.

Nevaeh pulled a notebook over and started listing numbers as products of primes, mostly to illustrate the pattern for herself. She wrote 12 as 2 times 2 times 3. She wrote 15 as 3 times 5, and 16 as 2 times 2 times 2 times 2. Every number she tried broke down into the same primes every single time, no matter which pair she split off first. It was like factoring had one right answer hiding underneath each number, and you couldn't see it until you dug.

"If 1 counted as prime, I could multiply by it forever," she typed slowly, working it out as she wrote. "like 12 could be 2x2x3, or 2x2x3x1, or 2x2x3x1x1. that's not one way anymore. that's a million ways."

"wait," Madeline replied. "so that's the whole concept? primes are the building blocks and 1 would break it?"

Nevaeh thought about her cousin at the picnic, how he'd tried to explain and she'd talked over him because she was sure she was right. She could have learned it that day for free. She turned back to the keyboard and found her loop, the one that checked every divisor from 2 up to the number itself. When the input was 1, the loop never ran at all, so nothing ever divided it evenly, and her code printed PRIME by accident. It wasn't a mysterious bug. It was a hole where a rule should be, and she hadn't known the rule.

She added a line at the top of the check: if the number was less than 2, print NOT PRIME. Then she typed 1, and the screen said exactly that. She screenshotted it and sent it to Madeline before she could second-guess herself, caption and all.

"tell your program mathematicians excluded 1 so every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes," she wrote. "or just steal my line of code."

"stealing the code," Madeline answered instantly.

Nevaeh grinned and hit run one more time, watching 1 flash its quiet little NOT PRIME across the screen.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Saying 'I'm sorry if you were upset' is often called a non-apology, because it expresses regret about the other person's feelings rather than about what the speaker did.
story:
Sawyer had typed and deleted the message nine times. The Reyes Family chat, six people, sat open on his phone: Mom, Dad, Grandma, his uncle, and Jerry, who was technically a cousin but functioned as a friend. He finally sent, "I messed up with Malaika. I said her volcano project looked like a kindergartner made it, in front of everyone, and now she won't sit with me at lunch. I have to fix it before Friday."

Dad replied first, while supposedly at work supervising three interns. "Tell her you're sorry if she got upset." Grandma sent a thumbs up. Sawyer copied the phrase, pasted it into his drafts for Malaika, and stared at it. Something about it itched. He read it aloud in his head, and itched worse.

The next morning Jerry sat with him on the bus, scrolling the family chat, which Sawyer had forwarded in desperation. "Your dad's version is bad," Jerry said. "Read it out loud." Sawyer did: "I'm sorry if you got upset." Jerry shook his head. "That's a non-apology. My sister calls everything that. It's sorry about her feelings, not about what you did. You're basically saying it's her fault for being upset." Sawyer looked at the sentence again and saw it, the way you see the trick in an optical illusion. The whole shape of it pointed away from him, toward her, as if she had done the reacting and that was the problem.

He became systematic about it. He wrote three drafts and tested each one the same way: did it name what he had done, and did it skip the word "if"? Draft one said he was sorry he had embarrassed her in front of the class about the volcano, which she had spent two weekends painting. Draft two added that the project was actually good and he had been showing off. Draft three got sent, with his stomach tight, at 7:42 p.m.

The reply came during dinner. His mom, across the table, watched his face change and raised an eyebrow, but said nothing, which he appreciated. Malaika had written: "The volcano took forever. Thanks for saying that. Sit with me tomorrow, but you're carrying my lunch tray for a week." He held the phone under the table so she wouldn't see him grinning.

He sent one more message to the family chat: "Fixed it. Dad's idea was a non-apology, Jerry says. Mine worked better." Dad's response arrived slowly, one bubble at a time: "Hm. I may owe your mother an edited message myself." Grandma sent a thumbs up, then, thirty seconds later, a single eye emoji.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: On a care label, an empty triangle means any bleach may be used, while a triangle with a cross through it means the garment must not be bleached.
story:
Tyler spent every Tuesday afternoon in the back room of the Ionescu Defensive Driving School, because his mother taught the seven o'clock class and somebody had to fold the towels. The school kept a washer and dryer behind the vending machines, and after a fender bender out front had flooded the storeroom with a small tsunami of mop water, Mr. Ionescu had declared that laundry would henceforth be Tyler's job. Tyler had agreed before understanding what he had agreed to.

The towels were easy. The problem was the stack of instructor shirts, white with thin blue stripes, which Mr. Ionescu was oddly attached to. One of them had a grease smear across the pocket from a lesson involving a stubborn hood latch. Tyler had already learned that hot water could be trusted with towels but betrayed him with the navy mat covers, which had come out blotchy and sad. He had learned to check pockets, too, after a tissue had shredded itself over everything. Now he wanted the grease stain gone, and on the shelf above the washer sat a bottle of bleach with a confident label.

Ashley, whose mother taught the Tuesday class too, was sprawled on the plastic chairs doing homework. "You're going to bleach a striped shirt," she said, without looking up.

"Stripes are white and blue," Tyler said. "It's basically a white shirt with ambitions."

"It's your funeral," said Ashley, which Tyler felt was an overstatement, but he checked the shirt anyway, because the last shirt he had ruined had cost him three weekends of vacuuming the training cars. Inside the collar there was a care label with a row of tiny symbols. One of them was an empty triangle. He held the sleeve of the other instructor shirts up next to it and found, on a grey pullover, a triangle with a cross through it.

"So this one means bleach is fine," he said, showing Ashley the empty triangle, "and the crossed-out one means no bleach. Ever."

"That seems like something the shirt should have told you earlier," Ashley said. She still hadn't looked up.

Tyler poured a careful capful into the dispenser, but he wasn't finished thinking. The grey pullover had a stain too, a coffee ring shaped like a small country. He could not use bleach on it, but the care label had other symbols he did not know. He laid all six instructor shirts out on the folding table and sorted them by label, building a system, feeling like the shirts had been carrying secret documents in their collars for years.

When Mr. Ionescu came back for his good shirt, it hung white and stripey and greaseless from the drying rack. He picked it up, held it to the light, and said nothing, which from him was a standing ovation. Then he pointed at the grey pullover, still stained, draped over a chair like an endangered species Tyler had failed to save.

"That one," Mr. Ionescu said, "you will figure out by Thursday."

Tyler looked at the crossed-out triangle on the label, then at the shelf, where the bleach sat beside a bottle of stain remover he had never opened.

"I'm on it," he said, and reached for the stain remover.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: 2 is the only even prime number, because every larger even number can be divided evenly by 2.
story:
The computer lab at Camp Wabaningo smelled like sunscreen and warm keyboards, which Noemie decided was the smell of learning something before lunch. Her task, written on the whiteboard by Mr. Murphy, was to build a Python program that asked for a number and printed whether it was prime. She had already typed most of it. The tricky part was the loop that tried dividing the number by everything smaller than it, which kept thwarting her with error messages about colons she was certain she had typed. She had not typed them.

"Your loop is skipping," said Emerson, leaning over from the next seat. He was wearing a plastic propeller cap he had won at the lake games, and the propeller spun whenever he jerked his head at her screen, which was often. "Also your hat is better than mine, and I resent that."

"It's not a hat, it's a fan," Noemie said, hitting run. The program asked for a number. She typed 7. Prime, it printed. She typed 9. Not prime. She typed 13. Prime. She raised both arms like she had just landed a canoe without tipping. Behind them, Gwen clapped twice, which was the lab's official applause ever since Mr. Murphy had banned whistling after the incident nobody would explain to new campers.

Emerson scrolled through her code with one assertive finger, not changing anything, just judging it. "Test 2," he said. "Small numbers break everything. My card trick broke on the number 2 once, and I never found out why, and it still haunts me."

Noemie typed 2. Not prime, the program printed. The room went quiet in the way a room does when a propeller stops spinning. "That's wrong," she said. "Two is prime. I'm sure of it." She stared at the screen. Nothing about the problem was visible; the code all looked the same as it had a minute ago, but somewhere in it a rule was hiding, and she intended to drag it into daylight.

She grabbed a scrap of paper and tried the program's logic by hand, the way Mr. Murphy had shown them when the debugger frustrated everyone. Divide by 2, divide by 3, divide by 4, and if any division comes out even, not prime. Then she stopped, pencil hovering. Her program divided 2 by 2, and 2 by 2 came out even, so her own program had talked itself out of the answer. And then a bigger thought arrived. Every even number bigger than 2 could be divided by 2 the same way, so all of them would fail, every single one. "Emerson. Two is the only even prime number. Everything even that's bigger just... can't be. It gets caught by the 2." She wrote a small fix on the paper, an exception for 2 before the loop even started, and moved it into the code.

She typed 2 again. Prime, the program printed, and Emerson's propeller spun wildly. Gwen leaned over her shoulder, eyes narrowing at the screen, and typed a number so long it scrolled off the input line entirely. The fan in the old computer began to hum.

"Gwen," Noemie said slowly, "what did you just give it?"

"Big enough to find out," Gwen said, and they all watched the cursor blink.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of children's bones, are weaker than the bone around them, which is why young athletes have limits on repetitive stress.
story:
Lincoln had been striking people out all afternoon, so when Coach walked to the mound and held up two fingers, he figured it was a sign for a curveball. It was not. "That's your pitch limit, kid. You're done for the day."

"You're counting wrong," Lincoln said, handing over the ball like it was a raw egg he didn't want to give back. "I've thrown maybe forty."

"Sixty-seven. Cael's been keeping the chart." Coach pointed to the fence, where Cael sat with a clipboard and a granola bar, looking entirely too pleased with himself.

In the dugout, Lincoln pulled his cap down over his eyes. Sixty-seven pitches felt like nothing. His arm wasn't even sore. Why would there be a rule for a problem he didn't have? He resented the chart, the count, the whole idea that a number on a clipboard knew more about his arm than he did.

Leilani sat down beside him and peeled her own orange in one long spiral, which she could do and he never could. "You look like a hawk stole your lunch," she said. "The guy batting cleanup has been giving you a predatory stare all inning, by the way. He wants your job."

"I had two more innings in me," Lincoln said. Then he thought about it. "Unless the rule isn't about how I feel today. Maybe it's about something I can't feel at all." He turned toward Cael. "Hey. Why sixty-seven? Why not a hundred?"

Cael shrugged. "Ms. Mokoena told me. Bones grow from cartilage near the ends, called growth plates. Growth plates are weaker than the bone around them. So kids' arms get limits on repetitive stress, like pitch counts. She made me memorize it before she'd let me keep score." He bit the granola bar with great dignity.

Lincoln flexed his elbow, trying to sense cartilage, which was like trying to hear your own blood. The weaker part was invisible, and it was exactly the part that made him him, still getting taller, still growing. "So the limit isn't for the me who feels fine today," he said slowly. "It's for the me who's still under construction."

"Weird way to say you're half-baked," said Leilani, and they laughed.

Last month he'd fallen off his bike and the nurse had checked the scrape for infection, and his mom had said something similar then, about growing bodies healing differently. He hadn't listened. He was listening now.

The game tightened up in the last inning, and the new pitcher loaded the bases. Cael appeared at the fence with his clipboard held high like a war banner. "Lincoln! I need you to chart foul balls. Official duty."

Lincoln grabbed a pencil and vaulted back toward the fence. "Sixty-seven's my limit, right? So what's the limit on foul balls?"

"Fifty," Cael said solemnly. "Fifty-one and we all go home."

"Better count fast, then," said Lincoln, clicking the pencil. "That cleanup guy looks hungry."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: The heart naturally speeds up a little on each breath in and slows down a little on each breath out, so slow breathing with long out-breaths helps the heart settle.
story:
Megan stood at the pharmacy counter waiting for her mom's prescription, her heart banging like a fist on a door. Tomorrow she had to give a presentation in Ms. Morin's class about the equator, and she had already fumbled it once, in front of everyone. Her friend Kale was beside her, buying ChapStick, watching her bounce on her toes.

"Your face is doing the thing," Kale said. "The red thing."

"I'm fine," Megan said, which was obviously not true. The blood pressure machine by the pharmacy window blinked at her, free to use, and on a wild impulse she sat down and slid her arm into the cuff. The numbers came up. Her pulse was 104, and she hadn't even climbed stairs.

An old man sitting in the waiting chair next to the machine was breathing in a slow, deliberate way, like he was doing it on purpose. She watched him. In through his nose while his chest lifted, out through his mouth for much longer. When the cuff squeezed her arm again, on a whim, she breathed the same way, stretched out the breath out until it felt like blowing out a hundred birthday candles one at a time. Her pulse read 96. She tried once more, this time paying attention to the beat itself, and noticed something odd: the thudding quickened a little each time she breathed in, then slowed a little each time she breathed out.

"That's what the pharmacist told me," the man said when he saw her staring. "The heart naturally speeds up a little on each breath in and slows down a little on each breath out. So I do slow breathing with long breaths out, and the heart settles." He demonstrated again, unhurried.

Megan tested it right there. Short, fast breathing made her pulse climb; long out-breaths let it sink, a few beats at a time. She thought about the week she'd had, the cumulative effect of three late nights and two botched practice runs and one presentation disaster. No wonder her heart had been sprinting. She couldn't see stress itself, but she could see its footprints on that little screen, and she could test whether her idea worked. It did.

That night she made a plan with her mom. She would prioritize sleep the way she prioritized homework: phone in the kitchen, lights out at nine thirty, same every night. Kale texted her a breathing reminder before class, just a picture of a candle with a long ribbon of smoke curling out.

At the pharmacy the next afternoon, picking up the same prescription, Megan sat at the machine again with Kale reading over her shoulder. Her pulse was 78. She breathed in, felt the small quickening, breathed out slow and felt the settling, and grinned.

"Seventy-eight," Kale read. "Is that good?"

"That's mine," Megan said, and pressed the button to run it again.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
story:
Riley sat on his bedroom floor with his phone face-down beside him, staring at the dilapidated model rocket on his shelf. Emerson had given him that rocket in sixth grade. Now Emerson walked past him in the hallway like he was furniture.

He picked up the phone, put it down, picked it up again. Three drafts of a text, all deleted. He remembered the fight in the cafeteria, two weeks back. Riley had laughed when Emerson missed the catch in gym class, laughed before he thought, and Emerson had gone quiet and stayed quiet.

In health class that morning, Ms. Adebayo had taped a poster above the whiteboard. Riley had read it twice while waiting for the bell. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, it said, mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being. Social. He'd chewed on that word all day. He'd been thinking of the fight as just a bad moment, but if friendships were part of mental health itself, then losing Emerson wasn't only sad. It was like losing sleep, or food.

"So it's not just feelings," he'd said to Delilah after class, tapping the poster. "Mental health includes your emotional, psychological and social well-being. The social part means friends count."

Delilah had shrugged. "Then go talk to him instead of orbiting my locker."

Now, in his bedroom, Riley formed a plan. His idea was simple: if Emerson was avoiding him, the cause wasn't the laugh itself. It had to be something Riley couldn't see, something under it. He tested the idea by scrolling their old messages. A pattern showed up fast. Every time Emerson mentioned the rocket club tryouts, Riley had changed the subject to basketball. Eight times in a month. Emerson hadn't signed up. The verdict, Riley decided, was that Emerson thought Riley found his whole interest embarrassing, and the laugh in gym class was just the proof he'd been waiting for.

Riley changed his mind about the text. No apology first. First, an offer.

He typed: "Rocket club tryouts close Friday. Come with me. I'll build one even if mine's terrible."

The reply took four minutes, which felt like four hours. "You'd do that?"

"Obviously. Bring tools. Mine has trust issues."

"Your rocket is held together with tape and regret," Emerson wrote back, and Riley could hear the grin in it.

Saturday morning, Emerson showed up at Riley's door with a toolbox and two kinds of glue. Riley's mom let them in and tried to console Riley about the ruined rocket, but he waved her off. In the bedroom, they spread newspaper across the floor.

"Two fins," Emerson said, holding up the pieces. "It needs two."

"Then give me the glue."

Emerson handed it over and sat down on the rug, close as ever, like the two weeks had never happened.

"Pass the tape," Riley said. "And the regret."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: A stuffy nose during a cold is caused mainly by swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose, not only by a buildup of mucus.
story:
Sydney had been sent to her grandmother's house with a box of tissues, a thermos of tea, and a nose that would not unblock. Grandma had gone to the market, so Sydney sat alone at the kitchen table, working through the tissues one by one. She blew her nose, hard, and felt exactly as blocked as before. She blew again. Nothing. It was like trying to empty a drawer that was too full of something she couldn't reach.

She called Bailey, who had missed the same cold by two days. "It's the worst part," Bailey said over the phone. "I thought blowing would fix it. I blew until my ears popped." Sydney looked at the pile of crumpled tissues, eleven of them, and felt pessimistic about tissue number twelve. "But that's the weird thing," she said slowly. "If it were just mucus in there, some of it has to come out eventually. Eleven tissues' worth came out. So why is my nose still completely blocked?" There was a pause on the line, the kind that meant Bailey was thinking the same thing.

Sydney went looking for evidence the way Grandma's old detective novels did it. She pressed one finger gently against the side of her nose. It felt puffed and warm, almost like a bruise. She remembered the word from a poster in the nurse's office: inflamed. And she'd once heard that a stuffy nose during a cold was caused mainly by swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose, not only by a buildup of mucus. If that was true, then blowing was like bailing water while the faucet was still running. The blockage wasn't sitting there waiting to be blown out. It was the nose itself, thickened from inside.

She had to test it. If the problem was swelling, then heat might be the answer, since Grandma put warm cloths on everything. Sydney filled a bowl with steaming water from the kettle, draped a towel over her head, and leaned in, determined to persevere even when her glasses fogged up completely. The steam crept into her nose, and for the first time in three days, air moved. Not much. A thread of it, then a little more. She sat up, breathing through one partly open nostril, grinning like she'd solved a bank robbery.

When Grandma came home, Sydney was still at the table, breathing loudly and triumphantly through half a nose. "You sound better," Grandma said, setting down her bags. "Steam," Sydney said, tapping the bowl. Grandma smiled, then frowned at the window. "Oh, dear. I was going to take you and Phoebe to the lake today, but with that cold still in you, I think it's soup and bed instead." Sydney looked at her one working nostril, then at the bright afternoon outside. She picked up the bowl. "Then I'm going back to the kettle," she said. "I have four more hours."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A small 2016 study by Binghamton University researchers found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one.
story:
Sophie sat cross-legged on Payton's bedroom floor with the group project between them: a small bridge made of brass rods, an alloy of copper and zinc that their science sheet said was more durable than plain copper. The bridge was due Monday. The text from Hayley, on Payton's phone, was due right now.

"Read it again," Sophie said.

Payton held the screen up. "Okay. I can't come. Sorry."

"She added Sorry, at least," Sophie said.

"She put a period after Okay. Look at it. 'Okay.' Who does that?" Payton set the phone down like it was warm. "She's mad we didn't prioritize the bridge over the weekend. That's what that period means."

Sophie wasn't sure a period could mean anything. A period was just how sentences ended, the way bridges ended at both banks. But Hayley had sounded fine at school on Friday, laughing about the coach's whistle, and now the message sat there with its little dot like a period at the end of a friendship.

"Try texting her something with a period," Sophie said. "Like an experiment."

"What do I even say?"

"Anything. 'The bridge looks good.'"

Payton typed, added a period, and sent it. Hayley replied in under a minute: "why do you sound weird"

Sophie borrowed Payton's laptop from the desk and searched "does a period in a text mean you're mad." The first real result was a study from 2016 by researchers at Binghamton University. They had found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one. The same words. Only the dot was different.

"Binghamton University," Sophie read out loud, "2016. Periods make texts look less sincere."

"So it's not just Hayley being dramatic?"

"It's not just Hayley being dramatic."

Payton picked up the phone and typed "sorry if the period seemed mad" without a period, then a second message, "that sounded weird also no period," then a third, "I'm going to stop texting now."

Hayley's reply took longer this time. When it came through, Payton's shoulders dropped with relief, and she turned the screen so Sophie could see it. "I wasn't mad. I was at my grandma's. She doesn't have wifi so I text slow and I always use periods because she taught me typing on a computer, also I have your bridge pieces in my backpack. I took them home Thursday."

Payton stared at the finished brass bridge between them, then at the message, then at the bridge again.

"Okay." She typed it with the period, hit send, and put the phone face down on the carpet.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Scooping flour straight from the bag packs it down, so a cup can hold much more flour than a recipe expects; weighing flour is more accurate.
story:
Grayson had promised his family fresh bread and cookies for Saturday dinner, and his first two batches had failed the same way: dry, cakey, heavy. He carried his grandmother's old recipe card to the farmers' market on Saturday morning because it called for farm-fresh eggs and honey, and because he wanted to solve the mystery before he embarrassed himself a third time.

At Mr. Yoon's flour stall, Zoey was there too, hovering over a shiny box on the counter. "My dad finally let me install the new scale today," she said, patting it like a pet. "I've been begging since spring. People kept arguing about whether our bags were honest, this whole flour-weight controversy, so now everything gets weighed in front of you." Grayson set his cloth bag on the counter and bought five pounds, but he didn't leave. He kept thinking about his cookie dough, which had felt stiffer than the recipe promised, and about how he always dug his measuring cup straight down into the bag.

"Can I borrow the scale for a second?" he asked. "Just a weird test." Zoey slid it toward him, delighted to have anyone use it. He scooped a cup of flour the way he always did, plunging the cup in and packing it tight, and weighed it. Then he poured that flour back, fluffed the rest with a spoon, and spooned a cup lightly into the measure, leveling it off. He weighed that too. The numbers were different, and not by a little.

Zoey leaned over the display. "That's so random. Same cup, same flour." Kyan, who had wandered over from the honey stall, asked what they were doing. "Testing something," Grayson said. "I think my cookies have been coming out dry and cakey because when you scoop flour straight from the bag, it packs down, so a cup can hold way more flour than the recipe expects." He weighed both cups again to be sure, and again the scooped cup came out heavier. "So the recipe's one cup isn't really one cup unless you weigh it. Weighing is accurate."

Zoey wrote the two weights on the back of his recipe card with a pencil stub. "For your bread too," she said, and she still looked proud of her scale. Grayson thanked them, tucked the flour under his arm, and walked home already planning: he would zero the kitchen scale with the bowl on it, weigh exactly what the card now said, and pull the cookies out a minute early.

That evening the kitchen smelled like actual bakery cookies, soft in the middle, and his father ate three before dinner. Grayson set the last one aside on a plate and called upstairs, "Come see what the scale did!"

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: The Gunnery camp, begun in 1861 by Connecticut schoolmaster Frederick W. Gunn, who led his students on a hike to a camp by the sea, is usually considered the first organized American summer camp.
story:
The camp brochure lay on Eva's bed next to her half-zipped duffel, and the bus came at eight, which gave her fifty minutes to pack, decide, and get downstairs.

"You're stalling," Marika said from the desk chair, tossing a rolled sock at her. "It's a duffel bag, not a hostage negotiation."

"I'm not stalling. I'm reading." Eva held up the brochure. "There's a page about the history of the camp. It says the whole idea started with something called the Gunnery camp."

Marika groaned. "You're going to speculate about summer camp history instead of packing your toothbrush. This is why we're friends. Nobody else would do this."

Eva read the paragraph again anyway. She had assumed camps were a modern thing, something invented for kids whose parents worked too much, maybe in the 1970s. But the page said the Gunnery camp was begun in 1861 by a Connecticut schoolmaster named Frederick W. Gunn, who led his students on a hike to a camp by the sea. And it said the Gunnery camp is usually considered the first organized American summer camp.

"That's older than basically everything," Eva said. "Older than light bulbs. Older than the car."

"Older than your running shoes, which still aren't in the bag." Marika pointed at them by the door.

Eva stacked the shoes on top of the sleeping bag and kept thinking. If the first camp was a schoolmaster taking his students on a hike, then camp wasn't invented to get rid of kids for the summer. It started as something a teacher wanted to do with them. She turned the idea over the way she'd test a rule in math class: if the cause was hidden, look at what it produced. A man walks his students to the sea, and a hundred and sixty years later there's a bus coming to Eva's corner with her name on a list.

She looked at the duffel, at the mirror over her dresser, at the duffel again. There was a kind of symmetry to it, she thought: a teacher once left a classroom for the shore, and now she was leaving her room for a lake. She tested the idea out loud. "So maybe everyone at camp is nervous the first time. Even the ones who look like they aren't."

"Or maybe you're stalling," Marika said, but she was smiling.

From the driveway came a honk, two short blasts. Mr. Sinclair leaned out of his truck window, keys in hand. "Your mom said you'd need a lift to the bus stop! I'm pulling out in five minutes, with you or without you!"

Eva swept the last stack of shirts into the duffel, sat on the zipper to force it shut, and grabbed the brochure off the bed.

"What do you need that for?" Marika asked.

"I want to read it on the bus," Eva said, and ran for the door.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Chinese, the word for 'four' sounds very similar to the word for 'death', so some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor.
story:
The elevator in Kamryn's apartment building had Ruby stumped from the moment the doors closed. She pressed the button for twelve and counted as the floors ticked past: three, five, six. "Where's four?" she asked, jabbing her thumb at the empty spot between the three and the five, as if the button might have evaporated and she could catch it reappearing.

"It's not a mistake," Kamryn said, shifting the gift bag to her other hand. "My grandma won't even say the number out loud. In Chinese, the word for four sounds almost the same as the word for death, so some buildings in East Asia just skip the fourth floor." Ruby stared at the row of buttons. The building did have a fourth floor, she realized; it was just hiding, wearing a five like a disguise. She had been riding elevators her whole life and never once thought a missing button could mean something.

Ruby was up here for a reason. Kamryn's grandmother was visiting from abroad, and Kamryn had invited her for tea, which meant Ruby had to get three things right: how to greet an elder, what gift to bring, and how to behave at the table. She thought back to last month, when she'd brought Ross a birthday present and he'd torn the paper off in three seconds flat while she stood there feeling oddly insulted. Later her mom had laughed and said some families open gifts later, alone, so nobody judges the giver or the gift. Ruby had changed her mind about wrapping paper that day: it was not just decoration, it was a message.

At the door, Kamryn nudged her, and Ruby remembered to hold her box of oranges out with both hands and to bow slightly instead of waving. Grandmother took it with both hands too, said something warm, and did not open it. Ruby kept sneaking glances at it on the side table all through tea. At the table she waited until Grandmother picked up her cup, then copied everything: turning her teacup, not sticking her chopsticks upright in her rice, keeping her elbows off the table even though at home nobody cared.

"You watch like a scientist," Kamryn whispered, and Ruby grinned, because that was exactly what she was doing, testing one rule at a time. The fatigue from staying so careful all afternoon hit her only when she got home and flopped on her bed, where she found the whole afternoon turning over in her mind like the tedious homework waiting on her desk. Maybe the fourth floor really was up there, numbered five. Maybe next weekend she would ask Kamryn to press three, then count the flights of stairs between doors, and find out.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Masaccio's Holy Trinity fresco in Florence, painted around 1427, is one of the earliest paintings built on a single vanishing point.
story:
Oliver sat at the kitchen table with a blank page in front of him and his dad's old print of a church fresco propped against the sugar bowl. He was supposed to draw a street for art class, one that looked like it went back into the distance, and every attempt so far had come out flat, like a map instead of a road. Landen had made his look easy yesterday, and Oliver hadn't asked how, which he was starting to regret.

He leaned close to the print. Ms. Hussain had shown it to the class and said something about it that Oliver had half forgotten, so he'd borrowed the print to look at it at home. She had said it was by Masaccio. The ceiling lines ran back toward the back of the painting, getting closer together. He touched the print with one finger, following a beam of the vaulted ceiling, then another beam. They weren't parallel. If he kept them going, they would run into each other somewhere behind the wall at the back.

"Are you drawing on that?" his dad asked from the doorway.

"Just tracing the ceiling lines," Oliver said. "With my finger." He kept going. Two lines met, and he tested a third one, from the floor, and then the pattern of the columns. Every line ran to one spot behind the painted altar. He grabbed a pencil and marked the point on the plastic sleeve, then sat back. "They all go to the same place."

His dad came over and looked. "Ms. Hussain told us this one's special," Oliver said, checking his memory of it. "It's the Holy Trinity, in Florence, painted around 1427, and it's one of the earliest paintings built on a single vanishing point." He didn't paraphrase it into something looser, because the date mattered, and anyway he wanted to say it right.

He turned back to his blank page. He drew a dot in the middle, then the edges of his street angling toward it, doors and windows getting smaller the closer they sat to that dot. It looked like a street. Not a competent one yet, he thought, judging the wobbly window ledges, but it went somewhere.

He heard his phone buzz and saw a text from Landen: you finish your street? Oliver typed back, come over tomorrow, I'll show you something. There was a pretty good probability Landen would argue about the dot, but that was fine. Oliver slid the print toward the middle of the table and tapped the pencil mark where all the lines crossed, one more time, just to be sure.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007, says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership.
story:
The group chat lit up at 9:42 on a Tuesday night, and by 9:45 Caleb had read the same argument three times without anyone actually saying anything new. Abdul had posted that his cousin Maya couldn't put "Anishinaabe" on her heritage project form because, in Abdul's words, "she isn't on the official list, so it doesn't count." Vera had replied in all caps that the list was nobody's business but Maya's. Then Abdul had sent a screenshot of some membership policy, and Vera had sent a single angry emoji, and now the chat was pinging so fast that Caleb's whole screen seemed to condense into a blur of blue bubbles.

He wanted to fix it before it got worse. He typed, deleted, and typed again, because anything he said would get screenshotted if it came out wrong. He could picture Maya at home, maybe watching her name get argued over by people who had never once asked her.

"Hold on," he finally sent. "Who says there's a list that decides this?"

Abdul answered first. "The band has rules. You're either on it or you're not."

"Maya told me she grew up going to her grandma's ceremonies every summer," Vera wrote. "That's more Anishinaabe than half the kids on some list."

"Doesn't matter," Abdul sent. "A list is a list."

Caleb stared at the words. He was thinking about the mock trial they'd done in Mr. Popescu's class, where the defendant's whole future had depended on which side got to define the argument first. Whoever defined the rules won. That was what was happening here, and nobody had noticed. Instead of typing another opinion, he opened a new tab and searched "who decides if you belong to an Indigenous group."

The first solid result made him sit up straight. He read it twice, then read it aloud to himself in the quiet of his room. He copied the link, pasted it into the chat, and typed underneath it: "United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted 13 September 2007. It says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership."

Nobody typed anything for a whole minute. The three dots appeared, vanished, appeared again.

"So the list isn't the final word," Caleb sent. "The peoples themselves decide who belongs. Not a form, not us."

"Wait," Abdul wrote. "That's actually a real thing? An actual UN thing?"

"Adopted on September 13, 2007," Caleb sent. "Look it up yourself if you don't trust my link."

Vera sent a row of exclamation points, and then a message that made Caleb grin at his ceiling: "Sending this to Maya RIGHT NOW."

At 10:03, a name Caleb hadn't seen in the chat for months appeared at the bottom of the screen. Maya had joined the group. Her first message was short: "Thanks. Can someone send me the link too?"

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: During the fight-or-flight response, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing speed up.
story:
The group chat lit up at nine that night, and Alexis read the messages with his stomach already twisting. Darcy: "presentation order is posted, Rahimi put me FIRST." Zayden: "brutal." Then his own name, third on the list, Wednesday morning. He typed back "ok," set the phone down, and noticed his heart was thumping like he'd sprinted up the stairs, even though he was just lying on his bed.

He picked the phone up again. "weird question. does anyone else's heart pound before presentations even though nothing is actually happening to you?" Zayden answered fast: "yes. every time. I thought it was just me being broken." Darcy sent a link from a health site she'd found for her own project on stress, and Alexis read it twice. Fight-or-flight, it said, and during it the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing speed up. So the pounding had a cause, a real chain from brain to glands to heart, and none of it meant danger. He screenshotted it.
