"But nothing dangerous is happening in Room 12," Zayden wrote. "unless you count Darcy's volcano model." "that model is ART," Darcy replied. Alexis thought about it, typing slowly. "I think it's like a smoke alarm going off when you burn toast. The alarm isn't wrong about what it's for. It just can't tell toast from a fire." Darcy sent three fire emojis and the words "radical idea: what if we practice on video call tomorrow so it's less like the first time we ever do it?"

Zayden expressed his skepticism in the way only Zayden could: "practice makes me MORE nervous, that's a known fact." But at seven the next evening all three of them were on a call anyway, notes propped against cereal boxes. Alexis's heart still hammered when Darcy said "go, you're up," but he tried something. He told himself the pounding was just adrenaline doing its job, then counted his breaths, four in, six out, until his breathing slowed and his heart followed. Zayden went second and mumbled through it, and Darcy made him go again, and the second try was steadier. "coping strategy acquired," Zayden announced. "do not get sentimental about it."

The night before Wednesday, Zayden sent eleven messages about quitting, and Alexis finally typed: "you can skip the call tomorrow if you really need to. that's a boundary, not a fail. but you'd have to do it Friday instead." He watched the typing dots start and stop three times before Zayden replied: "fine. but if I throw up on the slideshow, that's on both of you."

Wednesday morning, Alexis stood up third, and his heart did pound, and his breathing tried to quicken, and he let the adrenaline run its course like weather passing through. He got to the last slide without looking at his notes once. From the second row, Darcy held up her phone where he could see it, a message filling the screen: "SEE. TOAST, NOT FIRE."

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: The CSS rule h1 { text-align: center; } centres the text of every top-level heading on the page.
story:
Camille's screen showed her camp project, a page about the lake cleanup, with the big heading squashed against the left edge like it was hiding from the rest of the page. "Everything else is fine," she muttered. "Why does that look so wrong?" She leaned closer, breathing in the warm, dusty smell of the computer lab, and heard the fan whir under the desk. The camp's coding workshop had exactly three days left, and she wanted her page finished before the walkthrough on Friday.

Dereck slid his chair over, chewing a piece of spearmint gum so loudly she could hear it over the fan. "Mine did that too. I fixed it, kind of." He pointed at his screen, where his own heading sat in the middle. Camille squinted at his code and then at hers, trying to distinguish the difference between the two files. His stylesheet had a line hers didn't.

"You wrote that yourself?" she asked.

"Found it in the handout folder. It's a CSS rule, h1, curly braces, text-align: center."

Camille typed it in, saved, and refreshed her page. The heading hopped to the middle of the screen like it had been waiting for permission. "Whoa." She laughed out loud, and Kaiden, two seats down, looked over.

"What?" Kaiden said.

"It centres it," Camille said. "The rule h1, text-align center, centres the text of every top-level heading on the page."

"Every one?" Kaiden dragged his chair over so fast its wheels squeaked on the linoleum. He had five headings on his insect page, all shoved left. He typed the rule in and refreshed, and all five headings jumped to the middle at once, a whole lineup snapping into place. "That's kind of satisfying," he admitted.

Camille wasn't done, though. She had a smaller subheading on her page too, and it hadn't moved. She stared at the code, tapping her pen against her chin. The rule had changed only the top-level ones, the h1s. The subheading must be a different category, a different tag, so the rule skipped it. She tested it quickly, adding the same rule with h2 instead, and the subheading slid over to join the others.

Ms. Santos-Reyes walked past and paused at their row of monitors, three screens of perfectly centred titles. "Consistent layout," she said. "Nice work, you three."

Dereck popped his gum. "Team effort."

Camille saved her file twice, just to be sure, and hit refresh one more time to watch the heading hop.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Dermatologists advise reapplying sunscreen about every two hours outdoors, and right after swimming or heavy sweating, because it wears and washes off.
story:
David spread everything across his bed: sleeping bag, flashlight, the lucky water bottle he'd had since fourth grade. Camp started Sunday, two weeks at Lake Toma, and he'd never been away that long. His mother kept drifting past his door with suggestions he didn't ask for, and he kept pretending not to notice, because noticing meant admitting he was nervous.

Then the doorbell rang. It was Leandro, holding a red tube of sunscreen like it owed him money.

"You have to take this," Leandro said. "Two tubes. And a small one for your pocket."

David turned the tube over in his hands. "I already have sunscreen."

Leandro pulled up his phone and showed a photo from last summer: his own shoulders, blotchy and peeling, the skin across his nose tight and shiny. "That was after one afternoon at the lake. And I put sunscreen on that morning, before we even left the cabin. I never touched it again all day."

David sat down slowly on the sleeping bag. Something didn't fit. Sunscreen in the morning, sunburn by dinner. He'd assumed sunscreen was like a coat of paint, one layer and done. But Leandro had been in and out of the water all afternoon, sweating on the hike back. He thought about his own bottle at home, one big tube meant to last the whole trip, and began to understand why Leandro had bought pocket sizes. It wasn't extra; it was the whole point.

"So you have to put it on again," David said slowly, working it out. "Like, during the day. How often?"

Leandro shrugged. "My cousin looks this stuff up. She says every two hours outside. And right after you swim, or sweat a lot, because it wears off and washes off. She was pretty firm about the swimming part." He grinned. "You will swim. It's a lake."

They packed the tubes together, David integrating them into the side pockets where he could actually reach them, not buried under the extra socks. His mother appeared with a duffel and a hesitant look, as if she weren't sure she was allowed to help anymore, and David slid the bag toward her without a word. She smiled and started rolling his rain jacket.

That night David read the camp packing list one more time and copied a poem by hand, because Ms. Flores had told them to bring something from home to share at the campfire. He picked the shortest one, four lines, a single stanza about water, which seemed right for a lake. At the bottom of the page, under the poem, he wrote: "sunscreen, every 2 hours, after swimming." He underlined it twice.

Sunday morning his mother drove him to the bus. "Text me when you get there," she said, gripping the wheel.

"Only if my shoulders aren't red," David said, and held up the pocket tube so she could see it through the window as the bus pulled away.

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: In Buddhism, reaching nirvana ends the cycle of rebirth by ending the craving and ignorance that keep it going.
story:
The festival spread across the whole park, and Landon's chart was getting damp at the corners. He had folded his poster board in half to carry it, and now the crease looked brittle, like it might split if he opened it too fast. The assignment was due Monday: compare how two faiths explain what happens after death. He had picked Buddhism and Christianity because his grandmother was Christian and he wanted to understand what her minister meant by heaven, but the Buddhism column was nearly empty.

"Come on," Isabelle said, pulling his sleeve. "The food tables are by the lake, and Jagger's saving us dumplings." She was already halfway to the booth with the yellow banner, where a smiling woman was ladling soup into paper cups. Landon followed, chart under his arm.

Jagger waved them over. "There's a booth with incense and this giant wheel thing," he said through a mouthful. "Some guy at it kept saying people come back, like, over and over. Reborn. I didn't totally get it."

Landon stopped chewing. "Come back as what?"

"Doesn't matter. Come see."

The wheel turned out to be a painting of a circle divided into sections, animals and people and other figures all spinning around the rim. A teenage volunteer was explaining it to a small crowd, and Landon squeezed in close enough to hear her say the word "rebirth." So Jagger hadn't made it up. He copied the wheel onto the back of his hand with a pen, then asked the volunteer the question that had been obstructing him all week: "How does anybody get off the wheel?"

She smiled. "By reaching nirvana. Nirvana ends the cycle of rebirth."

"But how?" Landon pressed. "What actually stops it?"

"That's the part people forget," she said. "The cycle keeps going because of craving and ignorance. Nirvana ends the cycle by ending the craving and ignorance that keep it going."

Landon wrote it down word for word, feeling the click of a pattern fitting together. Back at the picnic table, he spread his chart flat and drew the wheel in the Buddhism column with an arrow breaking out of it. "See," he told Isabelle, "I kept thinking somebody had to escape, like climbing a fence. But it's more like the engine runs out of fuel." In the Christianity column he wrote his grandmother's word, heaven, and underneath it the line the minister always quoted about eternal life. Two different answers, but both of them about where the road ends.

Ms. Sandhu, his world cultures teacher, was judging the festival's student exhibits and paused at his table. She read both columns, then looked at the arrow breaking out of the wheel.

"Can you explain how the cycle stops?" she asked.

Landon took a breath. "In Christianity, it's eternal life with God. In Buddhism, reaching nirvana ends the cycle of rebirth by ending the craving and ignorance that keep it going." He tapped the empty space where the fuel had been. "Nobody has to climb anything. The wheel just stops."

Ms. Sandhu nodded slowly and moved on, and Landon turned back to his chart, drawing a small sun above the broken wheel. "You should show my grandma," Isabelle said. "She'd like the fence part."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Going to bed and waking up at about the same time every day, including weekends, helps keep the body's internal clock, called the circadian rhythm, steady.
story:
The note was folded into Violet's geometry binder, where Elissa always hid her messages, and it read: "You looked like a zombie in Mr. Liu's class today. Third time this week. What is going on with you?"

Violet read it twice under her desk. She had snapped at Liliane at lunch for no reason, and she had forgotten her gym uniform twice, and last night she had lain awake until one in the morning, her heart drumming over nothing she could name. On Saturday she had slept until noon, and Sunday too, because it felt like the only reward a hard week owed her. She scribbled a reply on the back of the note: "Meet me at my locker after last bell. I think I figured something out."

At the locker she laid out her evidence like a detective. "It's a pattern," she said. "Every Monday I'm a wreck, but Tuesdays are fine. Fridays I'm fine. It's only Mondays, and it coincides with the weekend, every single time." Elissa frowned and suggested maybe Violet just hated Mondays like everyone else. "No," Violet said. "My mom told me once that going to bed and waking up at about the same time every day, even weekends, keeps your body's internal clock steady. It's called your circadian rhythm." She snapped the locker shut. "So I'm going to test it. Same bedtime Friday and Saturday, even if my whole body screams."

The first weekend was torture. On Saturday night Elissa texted her a party invite, and Violet sat on her bed watching the little typing bubbles appear and disappear while the clock pushed toward ten. She typed "can't, sorry," set her alarm for the same time as every school day, and lay in the dark feeling like the only fourteen-year-old on earth choosing this. When the alarm rang Sunday morning she groaned into her pillow, but she got up.

Monday arrived, and Monday was different. She woke before the alarm, clear-headed, and in Mr. Liu's class she caught every step of the proof on the board. Afterward he stopped her at the door. "You've been more yourself lately," he said, and handed back her last quiz with a grade she hadn't seen since September. She floated through lunch. Even Liliane forgave her, splitting a cookie without being asked.

But there was a cost, and it showed up on Saturday. The group chat lit up with photos from a bonfire she had left at ten o'clock, right on schedule, and Elissa's caption said "wish you were here" with a photo of everyone's shoes by the fire. Violet looked at it for a long time. She was no longer exhausted, no longer snapping at people, no longer running on fatigue and bad temper; but she was also, apparently, the girl who went home early now. She tried to tell herself that sleep made her immune to jealousy, which was a lie, because she felt it anyway.

Still, the next Saturday, when Elissa asked if she was coming to the late movie, Violet hesitated only a moment. "I can do the early showing," she said, grabbing her jacket. "But I have to be home by ten."

"Your loss," Elissa said, but she was smiling as she linked arms with her, and they walked out into the evening together under the streetlights, Violet checking the time on her phone as they went.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Some element symbols come from Latin names, such as Fe for iron, from the Latin word ferrum.
story:
Max spread the periodic table across the kitchen table and weighed down the corners with two mugs and a stack of mail. The quiz was on Monday, and Ms. Kowalski had been clear about what it would cover: finding the number of protons in an element using its atomic number. Max wanted to get it right this time, because the last quiz had gone badly, and the mistakes on that quiz had been cumulative, one wrong idea stacking on the next until the whole page fell apart.

His plan was simple. He would go down the table and find iron, which had to be one of the easy ones. Everyone knew iron. He started at the top, scanning for an "I". He found I, sure, but that turned out to be iodine, which was not the same thing at all. He went back up and started again, slower this time, his finger drifting across rows of boxes. No other I. He checked twice.

"Dude, you're glaring at that paper like it insulted you," Pearl said, dropping her backpack on a chair. She'd come over to study, which mostly meant eating his family's snacks and occasionally being useful.

"Iron has no symbol," Max announced. "It's missing. It's not on the table. I've checked every single box."

Pearl leaned over his shoulder. "It's Fe. Right there. Twenty-six protons."

"Why would it be Fe? There's no F, there's no E, iron doesn't have an F sound anywhere in it. That box is mocking me." He tapped it accusingly. The atomic number 26 sat in the corner, bold and smug, and that part at least made sense. If the atomic number was 26, then twenty-six protons. That rule he had down cold.

"Maybe it's from another language or something," Pearl said, chewing a pretzel.

Max flipped the table over, where Ms. Kowalski had printed a small reference section. He ran his finger down the list and stopped. "Some symbols come from Latin names," he read slowly. "Like Fe for iron, from the Latin word ferrum." He sat back. "Okay. That's the weirdest thing I've heard today, and I watched a video of a hamster playing the piano this morning."

"So the periodic table is partly Latin," Pearl said. "That's actually kind of great. It's like a secret code."

"It's like a trap," Max said, but he was already hunting for more of them, and the hunt started to provoke real curiosity instead of frustration. Sodium was Na. Potassium was K, which honestly felt like cheating. Gold was Au, silver was Ag, and he began to see a symmetry in it, old names and new names sitting side by side in matching boxes, the whole table quietly organized by rules he hadn't known existed.

By the time Darcy texted asking what page the quiz covered, Max had made a stack of flashcards. He dealt them out like a card shark. "Fe," he said.

"Iron," Darcy said over speakerphone. "Twenty-six protons. Pearl drilled me on the bus."

Max grinned and flipped the next card. "Au."

"Gold. Seventy-nine. And don't even try to tell me there's no A in it, I already fell for that one."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: Every formula in Excel or Google Sheets begins with an equals sign; without it, the cell just shows what was typed as text.
story:
Hazel sat cross-legged on the kitchen floor with her mom's laptop balanced on the binder she used as a desk. The assignment from Ms. Do was due Monday: track one week of anything, build a spreadsheet, add a column with a formula, and make a bar chart. Hazel had chosen to track the birds at the feeder outside the window, because the backyard felt like its own little ecosystem and she liked the idea of counting sparrows in cells.

She typed her data into column B, one number per row: sparrows, chickadees, doves, jays. Then in the cell below the last number she typed SUM(B2:B10), because that was what Kameron had texted her yesterday. She pressed Enter. The cell said SUM(B2:B10), the exact words, not a total. Hazel frowned at it. She had typed it perfectly. Why would it just sit there like a label?

She tried again, deleting and retyping, slower this time, checking every letter. Still words, not a number. "That's not a total," she said out loud to the empty kitchen. Maybe Kameron had missed a step, or maybe she'd copied it wrong. She scrolled back through their messages. Kameron had actually written =SUM(B2:B10), with that little equals sign at the front. Hazel hadn't thought it mattered; it looked like decoration. She typed it again, this time starting with the equals sign, and hit Enter.

The cell showed 47. Hazel actually laughed. One character, and the whole thing came alive. So that was the rule hiding in there: the equals sign was how you told the program this is a formula, not just words. Without it, the cell showed only what she typed, plain text. She wondered what else was hiding like that, small marks doing significant work. She pulled up the chart tool and clicked bar chart, and there it was, sparrows towering over the jays, her whole week of counting turned into a picture.

Her phone buzzed. Kameron: "Stuck. My total just says the words again, help." Hazel grinned and typed back, "Start with the equals sign." A long pause, then: "Oh. Oh, that worked. You're a genius." She had been ready to blame Kameron for bad instructions, and now she felt bad about that, sitting there smiling at the screen instead.

The back door opened and her mom came in with groceries. "How's the project?" Hazel turned the laptop around, pointing at the bar chart, then at the little cell that read 47. "Watch this," she said, and typed the formula without the equals sign one more time, just to see the words appear where the number had been. "See? It's hiding in plain sight."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: The 800 metres draws on aerobic energy, which uses oxygen, and anaerobic energy, which works without oxygen but runs out quickly, so it feels like a sprint and a distance race at once.
story:
Everly stood at the far baseline of the basketball court, cones set at each corner, because Mr. Sok had said the perimeter was close enough to two hundred metres for practice. Robin stood beside her, and Evan leaned against the fence, spinning a ball on one finger like he had better things to do.

"Two laps for the eight hundred," Robin said. "Four corners, twice around."

"Four corners?" Evan pushed off the fence. "I run the hundred. I'll just go. Fast the whole way." He wore synthetic track shoes so bright they looked radioactive, and he jogged to the first cone like the race had already started.

Mr. Sok blew the whistle. Evan exploded into the lead, arms pumping, and by halfway around the first circuit he was ten metres clear. Everly held back, even though it hurt to do it, because she had a concept she wanted to test: that the race would give out energy in two different ways, one slow and steady, one quick and gone. Robin ran beside her, smooth and patient. "He's sprinting," Everly said between breaths. "Watch what happens."

At the start of the second lap, it happened. Evan's stride shortened. His shoulders climbed toward his ears. His bright shoes seemed to sink into the pavement, and Everly passed him at the far corner without changing her own pace. He finished thirty metres behind her, hands on his knees, gasping near the water bottles.

"That," he rasped, "was two races in one. It felt like a sprint and a distance race at the same time."

"That's exactly it," Everly said. She crouched beside him. "Robin told me there are two kinds of energy. Aerobic, which uses oxygen, and anaerobic, which works without oxygen but runs out quickly. You spent all your anaerobic in lap one. There was nothing left."

Evan looked at Robin, who was walking a slow cooldown lap along the sideline, untouched. "And you?"

"I run cross country. Aerobic is my whole life," Robin called back without stopping.

"So the second lap is where it's decided," Evan said slowly, as if the words cost him something.

Everly nodded. "First lap is just the ticket in." She set the cones up again. "Try it. Hold back on the first lap, even when you feel great, even when it seems wrong. Then see what's left."

Evan stood at the baseline again. The whistle blew, and this time he stayed level with Everly through the first corner, then the second, fighting his own legs the whole way, holding, holding. When they crossed into the second lap he surged, and this time his bright shoes stayed light on the court, and he beat her to the last cone by two strides, shouting loud enough to rattle the fence.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Glow sticks light up when bending breaks a glass vial of hydrogen peroxide inside, letting it mix with other chemicals and a dye in a reaction called chemiluminescence.
story:
Ruby sat on the bleacher edge of the gym, holding her phone low so the screen wouldn't glare across the dark floor, and read the family group chat by the light of it. Mom had sent a photo of the cat. Dad had sent a single thumbs up. Then Mr. Robinson, their neighbour, who had somehow ended up in the chat the day he helped them set up their Wi-Fi network, wrote, "Is the dance going well? We used to call it a sock hop. I realize that word is obsolete now."

"It's good," Ruby typed, then deleted it, because it wasn't quite good yet. The gym was strung with purple lights and half the eighth grade was already dancing, and Ruby had a bracelet of glow sticks on her wrist that refused to glow.

Zach dropped onto the bleacher beside her with his own pile of bracelets, handed to him at the door. "They gave me six," he said. He bent one, and it lit up green, so bright it lit his chin. He wanted to save the best ones, Ruby could tell, because he kept glancing toward the corner where a girl from his science class was dancing. "That one's for later," he said, laying the green bracelet carefully on his knee.

Zackery leaned over from the row below, frowning at the dark bracelet on Ruby's wrist. "Where's the light even coming from?" he asked, pointing at Zach's green one. "There's no battery in these things."

Ruby bent her bracelet again, harder this time, and felt a tiny crick inside, like a small piece of gravel snapping. She remembered a page she'd read in a science book at her grandmother's house, and an idea formed. "You have to actually break it," she said. "There's a little glass vial inside, full of hydrogen peroxide. Bending it snaps the vial, and then the hydrogen peroxide mixes with other chemicals and a dye. That's what makes the light." She cracked a second stick, felt the inner snap again, and the bracelet bloomed orange along its whole length. "The book called it chemiluminescence," she said, and held her wrist up next to Zach's.

"That's a real word?" Zackery said.

"Look it up if you want," Ruby said, but she was already testing it a third time, pressing a dead stick between her fingers until she felt the small break, and pink light spread from the spot like a slow blush. Three for three. It wasn't the batteries, it wasn't bad luck, it was just that the first snap hadn't been hard enough. She unclipped the orange one and held it out to Zackery, who threaded it onto his wrist and went back down to the floor holding his arm up like a lantern.

Ruby texted the group chat a photo of her glowing wrist. "Guess what's inside these," she wrote. Mr. Robinson answered within a minute: "Hydrogen peroxide, in a tiny glass vial. I read that in a magazine in 1974 and never had occasion to use it until now." Below his message, Mom sent a row of exclamation points.

The song changed to something slow. Zach stood up, took the green bracelet off his knee, and looked at the corner by the bleachers for a long moment. "Wish me luck," he said, and Ruby watched him cross the floor with the glow held out in front of him like something that could symbolize courage, or at least stand in for it. Zackery was spinning in circles with the orange one, drawing slow pink-orange circles in the dark. Ruby clipped two lit bracelets together, snapped the last dead one until it flared blue, and stepped down onto the floor herself, her whole arm a soft light.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses, so they do not help cure a cold or the flu.
story:
The kettle on her grandmother's stove rattled, and Julia pulled the quilt tighter around her shoulders, staring at the math homework she had no energy to do. She'd been at her grandmother's house since Tuesday, coughing and feverish, while at school the track team was deciding who would run the relay at the city meet. Romy had already texted twice. Coach permits only the top six to travel, Romy had written, and if Julia didn't get back by Friday, June would take her spot.

She remembered the last time she'd been sick like this, in fifth grade. She'd missed the class trip to the aquarium because she'd stayed home a full week, and afterward she'd wondered whether going back one day earlier might have saved her spot. Her grandmother had kept her in bed then, too, with honey tea and a humidifier that made the whole room smell like dust. Julia had never quite decided whether her grandmother had been right to be so strict.

She shuffled into the kitchen, where her grandmother was chopping ginger, and made her case. "Can we call the doctor? If I get antibiotics, I bet I'd be better by tomorrow." Her grandmother gave her a long look, then handed her the phone and said Dr. Osei would do a phone call after lunch.

Dr. Osei was brisk and kind. When Julia asked for the antibiotics, he chuckled, not unkindly. "They kill bacteria," he said, "but a cold or the flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics have no effect on viruses. They won't help you get better faster." Julia slumped against the counter. So there was no shortcut. Only rest, fluids, and time, which meant Friday was a dream and June would run.

After the call, she sat by the window watching a woodpecker hammer at the old maple. The bird's beak, she thought, was an adaptation for exactly that job, and hers, apparently, was a body that healed slowly whether she liked it or not. She tried to estimate when she'd be well enough to walk to the corner without getting dizzy. Her answer was approximate at best, maybe Saturday, maybe Monday.

She texted Romy: "Tell June she's in. Tell her to run the third leg like it's hers, because it is." Then she found her grandmother in the garden and asked whether she'd missed the aquarium trip all those years ago too. Her grandmother only smiled and said, "The aquarium is still there. Races aren't." Julia wasn't sure if that was a lesson or a confession, and her grandmother didn't say.

On Saturday morning the fever had broken, and Julia stood in the backyard with a blanket over her shoulders, breathing cold air that finally didn't scratch. Romy sent a video of the relay, June surging on the third leg, the team taking second by half a stride. Julia watched it three times, then held the phone out toward her grandmother. "Look at her go."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Carbon has atomic number 6, so every carbon atom has six protons in its nucleus.
story:
The garage smelled like motor oil and old carpet, but Cameron had claimed it as his study fort since September, when his mother agreed to enroll him in the school's science team. The first meet was in five days, and the events list had one word that made his stomach flip: chemistry. He spread the periodic table across the workbench and pinned its corners with four bolts.

Stefano ducked under the half-open door, Alexandre behind him, carrying a bag of chips and his own crumpled copy of the table. "Ms. Ortiz says the whole first round is atomic numbers," Stefano said, dropping onto an overturned milk crate. "They give you an element, you give them the protons."

"That's impossible," Cameron said. "You can't count things that small. Nobody can see a proton."

Alexandre shook the chip bag open. "So we figure out the trick." He pulled a pencil from his backpack and tossed it onto the bench. "Start there. The label says graphite. Ms. Ortiz mentioned graphite is carbon."

Cameron picked up the pencil and found the fine print. Then he hunted down carbon on the giant table, dragging his finger across the squares until he hit the letter C. Above the symbol sat a small bold number: 6. He stared at it, then at the pencil, then back at the table. "Wait. Carbon has atomic number 6, so every carbon atom has six protons in its nucleus." He said it slowly, testing the sentence the way you'd test a wobbly board before stepping on it. "The number and the protons are the same thing. It's not a trick. It's a rule."

"Prove it," Stefano said, grinning, and grabbed the chips. "Name an element."

Cameron covered the symbol with his thumb. "Oxygen, atomic number 8, so eight protons. Gold, 79. Hydrogen, 1." Alexandre checked each one against his crumpled copy, calling out yes, yes, yes like a referee.

They drilled until the garage light went dim, taking turns quizzing each other, laughing when Cameron said iron had 24 protons and had to recheck the square twice before muttering twenty-six. Stefano was quizzing him on helium when a knock rattled the side door. It was Ms. Ortiz, holding a clipboard, checking on the team's practice logs before Saturday. "How's it going in here?" she asked.

Cameron lifted the pencil like a trophy. "Every carbon atom in this graphite has six protons. Want to bet the judges ask about it?"

She smiled and wrote something on her clipboard. "No bet," she said. "Just don't drop the pencil."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: The 'fundamental attribution error', named by psychologist Lee Ross in 1977, is the habit of blaming someone's behavior on their character while overlooking the situation they were in.
story:
Ariana set her tray down at the far end of the table, away from where Mika usually sat. For three days she had eaten like this, in the middle of the cafeteria noise, alone on purpose. Mika had skipped her birthday sleepover, and that was the whole story as far as Ariana was concerned. You don't ditch your best friend's thirteenth birthday, a night planned for a month, unless you simply don't care.

Kohen slid in across from her, holding the yearbook layout notebook they were both supposed to sign off on by the end of lunch. "We have twenty minutes to approve the friendship page," he said. "Yours and Mika's is the big one. Half a spread."

"Then cut it," Ariana said. "She bailed on my party with some lame text. That's who she is."

Kohen turned his pudding cup slowly, like he was buying time. "In psych class Ms. Khoury had us read about this. It's called the fundamental attribution error. Named by a psychologist, Lee Ross, in 1977. It's the habit of blaming someone's behavior on their character while overlooking the situation they were in."

"Meaning I'm wrong because I'm mad?"

"Meaning maybe you don't know the situation." He nudged the notebook toward her. "I saw her in the hallway yesterday. She looked lethargic, like she hadn't slept. That's not the face of someone who doesn't care."

Ariana turned the idea over the way she turned a puzzle piece, testing whether it fit. Her assumption had felt like a fact: Mika is selfish, therefore she skipped. But if the assumption was wrong, the whole chain collapsed. There was a cheap way to test it, too. She picked up her tray, walked the length of the cafeteria while Kohen watched, and stopped at Mika's table.

"You missed my party," Ariana said. "Before I decide what that means, tell me why."

Mika's eyes went glassy. "My grandma had a stroke that afternoon. We drove four hours to the hospital. I couldn't even text properly, I was so tired. I thought you'd figure I'd explain later."

"You could have led with that."

"You could have asked." Mika wiped her eyes with her sleeve. "Is your page in the yearbook still ours?"

Ariana checked the clock above the serving line. Twelve minutes left. "Come sign it with me right now," she said, and pulled Mika up by the wrist, half running past Kohen, who was already flipping the notebook open to their spread.

"You two have fun being sentimental," he called. "I'll clarify the captions."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In experiments by psychologist Henri Tajfel, people favoured members of their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random.
story:
Lucas arrived at the community centre early to claim the good easel, the one by the window where the light came in flat and honest. Mr. Adebayo was setting up the summer mural project in the big hall, and today he was splitting everyone into four teams. "Fair way," he said, holding up a bucket. "Names go in, names come out. Pure chance." Lucas watched him fold the slips, drop them in, and shake.

The draw put Lucas with Aurelie and a group of kids from the west side of town, while Merrick landed on Team Blue across the hall. Merrick had wanted Lucas on his team all week, because Merrick wanted to win the mural contest more than anything, even though the only prize was choosing where the mural hung. Within an hour, Team Blue was chanting, hoarding the best paints, and claiming the wall with the most sun. Aurelie rolled her eyes, then started hoarding brushes on her side. By the next morning the teams were trading insults over the tape line down the middle of the floor, and Lucas could not figure out why. Nobody knew each other. Nobody had picked their teams. The groups had been assigned completely at random, and it made no sense that random groups would act like rivals.

He tested it. At lunch he quietly told three kids on his team that he had heard Team Blue was assigned randomly, by drawing names from a hat. It changed nothing; they still guarded the brushes. So he went further. He borrowed Mr. Adebayo's list and made everyone's assignment public, showing that the only criterion for who was on which team was luck. Aurelie studied the list, then looked at the tape line. "We're fighting over a hat," she said slowly. "The hat decided." Lucas nodded. He had found a book in the centre's small library the night before, about a psychologist named Henri Tajfel, whose experiments showed that people favoured members of their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random. The hall was proving it, wall to wall.

Lucas asked Mr. Adebayo to mediate, not by punishing anyone but by letting the two teams propose a joint design for the single big wall instead of two small ones. Aurelie presented it, since she wanted credit for the idea and had earned it. Merrick protested at first, then admitted that a mural he only half-owned still beat a small one he fully owned. The kids from the west side shared their paints, and by Friday the tape line was peeled up and forgotten.

The finished mural showed four pairs of hands passing a bucket between them. Everyone agreed it was the best thing the centre had ever displayed. On Saturday morning Lucas came in and stopped in the doorway: someone had drawn a neat line down the middle of the mural with pencil, and beside it, in Merrick's handwriting, a small note. "Our half is still better."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Crying when a parent leaves is called separation anxiety; it is a normal stage of development that commonly begins in the second half of a baby's first year.
story:
Stella stood in Ms. Brennan's kitchen with a list of emergency numbers on the fridge and a ten-month-old baby named Robin squalling in her arms. Ms. Brennan and her husband were barely out the door, and Robin's face had gone from pink to a furious purple.

"It's okay, it's okay," Stella said, bouncing her the way her mom did with her cousin. Robin screamed louder. Stella checked her diaper, offered a bottle, held up a stuffed elephant. Nothing worked. Ten minutes of this, and Stella's arms were shaking.

She pulled out her phone and texted Abygael, whose little brother was two. HELP. Baby won't stop crying. Parents just left.

Abygael texted back fast. My mom calls it separation anxiety. It's a normal stage of development. Started for my brother around seven or eight months, in the second half of his first year. He screamed every time Mom left.

Stella read the message twice. So the crying wasn't about hunger or a wet diaper or anything she'd missed. It was about the parents walking out, and if that was the cause, then maybe it had a pattern too. She remembered Abygael's next text arriving a second later: It fades once he gets distracted by something fun. Distraction was her hypothetical fix, and there was only one way to test a hypothesis.

She carried Robin to the kitchen window, where the feeder hung over the herb pots. "Look," Stella whispered, tapping the glass. A goldfinch dropped onto the perch. Robin hiccupped, went quiet, and stared. When the bird flew off, Stella shook a plastic cup of dry pasta from the drawer, and the rattle turned the sobs into a slow, wobbling smile. The crying dwindled to sniffles, then to nothing at all.

An hour later, Robin sat on the kitchen floor banging the pasta cup while Stella texted Abygael a thumbs-up. Ms. Brennan and her husband came through the back door at nine, looking worried and ready to apologize. Instead they found Stella cross-legged on the tiles, making the elephant dance while Robin shrieked with laughter.

"She cried when you left," Stella reported, standing up. "Separation anxiety, apparently. Totally normal for her age. But it faded once we started having fun."

Ms. Brennan pressed a hand to her chest. "You figured that out yourself?"

"With backup," Stella said, and showed her the texts. Ms. Brennan laughed and slid an extra five dollars into Stella's hand, calling the crying-bird-rattle routine a small miracle, though Stella privately considered it less a miracle than an anomaly of timing: the one night she panicked was the one night everything worked. On the walk home, she was already planning to ask if she could babysit again next Friday, pasta cup in her backpack, just in case.
